title: Saturdays
note: Fictional patient. Clinical questions belong to the nurse and nephrologist; your agency’s and unit’s policies come first.
intro: You are the unit’s social worker. Mrs. Gina Torres, 52, has been on hemodialysis for a year on Tuesday, Thursday, and Saturday. She has missed three Saturday sessions this month. The referral note says: “Noncompliant. Counsel.” You meet her on Tuesday before her session. She crosses her arms. “Are you here to scold me too?”

choices.text: “It sounds like you’ve had a lot of that. I’m not here to scold. I’d like to understand what Saturdays are like for you.”
choices.feedback: Agree with what is true, step away from the lecture, and ask an open question. Partnership and acceptance come before any plan.
choices.then: She uncrosses her arms. Her husband is paid on Mondays, so by Saturday there is no money for the tricycle and jeepney. On Saturdays she also minds her granddaughter while her daughter works. And she stopped her phosphate binder because “it burns my stomach.”

vitals.barriers: Fare before payday; childcare; binder heartburn

choices.text: “You need to understand that missing dialysis can kill you.”
choices.feedback: This is the righting reflex. She has heard it before, and it makes people defend the status quo. Ask about her experience instead.
choices.then: She goes quiet. You change course and ask what Saturdays are like. She tells you about the fare, her granddaughter, and the binder that burns her stomach.

vitals.barriers: Fare before payday; childcare; binder heartburn

choices.feedback: Direct, but “why” can sound like an accusation. An open, curious question about her Saturdays invites a story.
choices.then: Hesitantly, she tells you about the fare, her granddaughter, and the binder.

vitals.barriers: Fare before payday; childcare; binder heartburn

n2.prompt: How do you handle the three barriers?

choices.text: Fare and childcare are practical barriers you own with the head nurse (transport help, a different day or shift); the binder heartburn is a belief and side-effect question for the nephrologist and pharmacist, so you tell them today.
choices.feedback: Every behavior has a reason. Name each reason’s type and send it to its owner. A side effect is a clinical question, not a motivation problem.

vitals.owners: Fare/childcare: SW + head nurse; binder: nephrologist

choices.text: Tell her the binder is safe and she must restart it, then work on the fare.
choices.feedback: Whether the binder is right for her, and what to do about the heartburn, is the nephrologist’s and pharmacist’s decision. Route it; do not prescribe.
choices.then: You route the binder question to the nephrologist and work on the practical barriers.

vitals.owners: Fare/childcare: SW + head nurse; binder: nephrologist

choices.text: Arrange fare assistance; the rest will follow.
choices.feedback: Fare help is a real fix, but the childcare and the binder would still keep her away or unwell. Address each barrier.
choices.then: You also raise the childcare with the head nurse and the binder with the nephrologist.

vitals.owners: Fare/childcare: SW + head nurse; binder: nephrologist

n3.scene: She says: “Maybe I could come on Saturdays if someone watched the baby.”

choices.text: “So if the baby were looked after, coming on Saturday would feel possible. Who might be able to help with that?”
choices.feedback: That is change talk. Reflect it and draw out more; the plan is stronger when the idea is hers.
choices.then: She thinks her sister-in-law could watch the baby, if the session started later.

choices.feedback: Jumping to a commitment skips the barrier she just named. Reflect and explore first.
choices.then: She shrugs. You go back and ask who might help. Her sister-in-law could, if the session started later.

choices.feedback: Arguing with her values pushes her toward sustain talk. Her granddaughter matters to her; work with that.
choices.then: She looks away. You reflect what she said and ask who might help. Her sister-in-law could, if the session started later.

vitals.owners: Later Sat shift requested; fare assistance applied

n4.prompt: How do you rewrite the referral note?

choices.text: “Missed three Saturday sessions this month because of no fare before payday and Saturday childcare. Stopped binder because of heartburn; referred to nephrologist. Later Saturday shift requested; fare assistance applied for.”
choices.feedback: Write what happened, how often, and the person’s reasons. “Noncompliant” describes the team’s frustration and hides the reason, which is the only thing that leads to a solution.
This tells the next reader nothing they can act on, and labels her.
Closer, but vague. Name the specific barriers, the binder referral, and the plan.

n5.scene: Two months later she comes most Saturdays. She still plans to miss one Saturday a month for her granddaughter’s school events. The nephrologist has explained the risks, and she can explain them back.

choices.text: Check she understood, make sure the nephrologist knows her decision, record it with the information given, and keep the door open.
choices.feedback: When an informed adult chooses differently, respect it, record it, and stay in relationship. People change their minds when they feel respected, rarely when they feel cornered.

choices.text: Ask her daughter to make her come, and warn that missed sessions will be reported.
choices.feedback: Pressure and threats damage trust and often increase missed sessions. Enlisting the family to coerce her is not support.

choices.text: Close the case; she has made her choice.
choices.feedback: Respecting a choice is not the same as stepping away. Keep the relationship open; her circumstances and her mind may change.

end.title: Three months on
end.text: The later Saturday shift and fare assistance hold. The nephrologist changed her binder and the heartburn settled. She misses one Saturday most months, as she decided, and the nephrologist adjusts her plan around it. Her chart now says why.

debrief:
What this case teaches

  • Behavior has a reason. Replace “noncompliant” with what happened and why.
  • Resist the righting reflex. Agree with what is true, ask open questions.
  • Name each barrier’s type and owner: practical to you, symptoms and medicines to the clinicians.
  • Reflect and draw out change talk.
  • Respect an informed choice, record it, and keep the door open.

See Behavior has a reason, Walk beside, What to strengthen and Respecting an informed choice.
